source.title: An Empirical Study of Memorization in NLP

record.tranche_reason: Tests the effect of removing highly memorized training examples on held-out performance, extending the image-classification finding to NLP datasets and CIFAR-10 with a different memorization measure.
record.gate_note: The study reports retraining results after removing top-ranked memorized examples or the same number of random examples. Token attribution and instance-typicality findings do not directly test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares held-out accuracy after removing highly memorized versus equally many random training examples and retraining. It extends V8 to NLP and CIFAR-10, using influence-function self-influence rather than the original inclusion-based memorization estimator.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the authors' conclusion that their experiments validate the long-tail theory on three NLP datasets and show memorization can help generalization. They also conclude that their attribution method helps explain memorization. CIFAR-10 serves as a check of their alternative memorization score.
record.recipe_differences: Follows the removal-and-retraining experiment used by Feldman and Zhang, but uses self-influence based on the influence function of Koh and Liang to rank memorized examples; reports NLP datasets and CIFAR-10.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset changes the tested setting; the paper reports separate removal comparisons for SST-2, Yahoo! Answers, SNLI and CIFAR-10. Removal fraction is varied in Figure 1.

fits_no_version.finding: Highly self-influential examples appear atypical in SST-2 and SNLI; SST-2 also has a phrase-based quantitative comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High self-influence identifies atypical training examples in these tested NLP settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Masking highly attributed tokens or image features reduces measured self-influence more than random masking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization attribution identifies input features whose removal disproportionately reduces self-influence.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative SST-2 and CIFAR-10 examples associate high memorization attribution with features negatively correlated with the correct label.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features conflicting with an example's class can receive high memorization attribution.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), 2022
record.problems: For the test-accuracy removal comparisons, most values are presented in Figure 1 rather than stated numerically in the text. The study reports averages and standard deviations over five retraining runs, but the supplied text does not give the numerical standard deviations. The authors note that influence scores are model-dependent and compute them from a single checkpoint for the main experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified per-removal-fraction values were added for the plotted curves because the text provides no exact values and the figure is not available as extractable numeric data. The token-removal attribution results measure change in self-influence rather than the held-out accuracy effect in V8, so they are described under fits_no_version rather than added as V8 rows.

untested.parts: No comparison of random-label fitting with natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or test of generalization beyond interpolation.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or comparison of generalization measures.
Does not test the original inclusion-based memorization estimator, end-to-end ResNet-50 on CIFAR-100 or ImageNet, or the smaller effect on MNIST.

record.verdict_notes: Support concerns removal effects under the study's self-influence proxy; it does not establish equivalence to the original estimator or independently prove memorization is necessary. Figure-only numerical values are already declared omitted. Qualitative result statements suffice to establish direction, but do not establish statistical significance at every removal fraction.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting random labels with generalization on natural labels.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected architectures.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-measure comparison.
Tests removal of top-ranked memorized examples versus random removal on SST-2, Yahoo! Answers, SNLI and CIFAR-10; does not test ResNet-50 on CIFAR-100 or ImageNet, or the stated MNIST qualification.

rows.subject: Distill-BERT
rows.size_stated: 6 transformer layers; each layer consists of 12 attention heads
rows.stage_stated: fine-tuned; word embedding layer and first 4 transformer layers frozen, last 2 transformer layers and final projection layer fine-tuned
rows.operation_detail: Remove the top-ranked memorized training instances during training and retrain; compare with removing the same percentage of random training instances.
rows.measure: Marginal utility on test accuracy, expressed as the test-accuracy drop attributable to removing the selected examples.
rows.baseline: Random subset of 30% of training examples: 0.70 percentage points
rows.value: Top-30% memorized training examples: about 1.44 percentage points
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation shown in Figure 1; numerical value not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports this example explicitly; the comparison is the drop in test accuracy, not raw test accuracy.
rows.check: The reported drops are correctly recorded: about 1.44 versus 0.70 percentage points. Memorization ranking uses infinitesimal downweighting effects on own-label probability, a proxy for V8's inclusion-based definition. Normalize the model name to DistilBERT.
